title: Phrasal Verbs with Up: Progress, Beginnings and Outcomes
summary: Use phrasal verbs with up to describe approaching or keeping pace with others, starting organisations and hobbies, growing up, tidying spaces, and reaching results. Distinguish catch up, keep up, set up, take up, end up and give up, with accurate object positions.
learningObjectives: Explain approaching and matching someone’s pace using come up, catch up with and keep up with.
Use set up, take up and fix up for establishing organisations, starting activities and arranging meetings.
Describe growing up, raising children, tidying and washing dishes using common up expressions.
Express unexpected outcomes, quitting, arrival, composition and complete use of resources with up phrasal verbs.

explanation.heading: Approaching, reaching and maintaining pace
explanation.body: Come up, go up or walk up to somebody or something means approach. Catch up with someone means move faster until you reach them; catch someone up is also possible in some varieties. Keep up with means remain at the same speed, level or rate, even when a task is difficult. Use with to identify the person or standard you are following.
explanation.example: The tourists walked up to the information desk to ask about tickets.

explanation.heading: Starting an organisation, a hobby or an arrangement
explanation.body: Set up a club, organisation, business or system means establish it and make it ready to function. Take up a hobby, sport or activity means begin practising it regularly. Fix up a meeting means arrange it, usually in informal English. Set up and fix up take objects; with a pronoun, say set it up or fix it up.
explanation.example: A group of neighbours set up a weekend gardening club.

explanation.heading: Growing up, bringing up children and cleaning up
explanation.body: Grow up describes becoming older and reaching adulthood. Bring up a child means raise and care for the child; the two are different perspectives. Tidy up, clean up and clear up can describe making a place neat or removing a mess. Wash up is commonly used in British English for washing dishes after a meal.
explanation.example: After the shared dinner, the guests helped wash up in the kitchen.

explanation.heading: End up, give up and show up
explanation.body: End up + -ing or end up + place/result reports the final outcome of a situation, sometimes unexpected. Give up means stop trying or abandon an activity; give something up is also common. Show up or turn up means arrive or appear, especially when someone was expected. With a pronoun object, say give it up, not give up it.
explanation.example: We missed the last bus and ended up walking back to the campsite.

explanation.heading: Using resources, taking space and making up a group
explanation.body: Use something up means consume all of it, leaving none. Take up time or space means occupy it. Make up can describe what proportion or part of a whole a group forms; be made up of identifies the components of a whole. These are different from inventing a story with make up, which belongs to the next lesson.
explanation.example: Local residents make up almost half of the volunteers at the shelter.

left.label: catch up with
left.example: Noah accelerated and caught up with the cyclists.
left.note: He had been behind, then reached them.

right.label: keep up with
right.example: Noah kept up with the cyclists for the next hour.
right.note: He maintained their speed and did not fall behind.

left.label: set up
left.example: They set up a neighbourhood recycling scheme.
left.note: They established an organisation or working arrangement.

right.label: take up
right.example: They took up swimming in the summer.
right.note: They began practising a sport or hobby.

left.label: end up + -ing
left.example: We ended up eating at the station café.
left.note: This was the outcome of the situation.

right.label: give up + -ing
right.example: We gave up trying to find the original restaurant.
right.note: We deliberately stopped attempting an activity.

left.label: take up
left.example: The display takes up a whole wall.

right.label: use up
right.example: The workshop used up all the spare batteries.
right.note: The available supply was completely consumed.

examples.sentence: Jules came up to the counter and asked for a timetable.
examples.note: Come up to indicates movement towards a person or location.

examples.sentence: It was hard to keep up with the rapid changes in the timetable.
examples.note: Keep up with can refer to maintaining the same rate or level, not only walking speed.

examples.sentence: The community centre fixed up an introductory meeting for new members.
examples.note: Fix up means arrange a meeting.

examples.sentence: After moving abroad, Salma took up painting in her spare time.
examples.note: Take up an activity means begin doing it as a hobby.

examples.sentence: My father grew up on an island, and his grandparents brought him up there.
examples.note: Grow up describes the child’s development; bring somebody up describes raising the child.

examples.sentence: The caretaker asked us to tidy the room up before leaving.
examples.note: Tidy up is separable when it takes a noun object.

examples.sentence: Only twelve participants showed up for the early workshop.
examples.note: Show up means arrive or appear, particularly when expected.

examples.sentence: The whole orchestra is made up of students from several schools.
examples.note: Be made up of introduces the parts that form a whole.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I cannot keep up the other runners.
commonMistakes.correct: I cannot keep up with the other runners.
commonMistakes.why: Keep up with somebody requires with to name the person whose pace you match.

commonMistakes.incorrect: They set up it before the opening ceremony.
commonMistakes.correct: They set it up before the opening ceremony.
commonMistakes.why: In separable set up, the pronoun object it must come before up.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She took on astronomy as a new hobby last winter.
commonMistakes.correct: She took up astronomy as a new hobby last winter.
commonMistakes.why: Take up a hobby means begin pursuing it; take on does not express that standard hobby meaning here.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I gave up to learn the violin after two difficult lessons.
commonMistakes.correct: I gave up learning the violin after two difficult lessons.
commonMistakes.why: Give up an activity is followed by an -ing form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The class used up them during the art project.
commonMistakes.correct: The class used them up during the art project.
commonMistakes.why: A pronoun object goes between used and up.

studyTips: Make two timelines: catch up means reach someone after lagging behind; keep up means avoid falling behind.
Learn set up a project and take up a hobby as separate verb–noun partnerships; use each in a fresh sentence.
Compare grow up (child’s development) and bring up (adult’s care) with the same family scenario.
When a phrasal verb is separable, substitute it or them to practise the obligatory middle position.

exercises.prompt: After several months of planning, the volunteers ___ a free weekend reading club.
exercises.feedback: Set up means establish an organisation or club and make it ready to operate.

exercises.prompt: Nico had never played chess before, but he ___ the game as a new hobby at university.
exercises.feedback: Took up the game means Nico began practising chess as a new hobby.

exercises.prompt: The guide walked very quickly, and I could not ___ her on the steep path.
exercises.feedback: Keep up with someone means move at the same speed as that person.

exercises.prompt: These enormous storage boxes ___ too much space in our small office.
exercises.feedback: Take up space means occupy it, not consume or create it.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday the class ___ all the coloured paper during the project. (use up; past simple)
acceptedAnswers: used up
exercises.feedback: Used up means the entire supply of paper was consumed.

exercises.prompt: When the evening lecture was cancelled, we ___ studying together in the library. (end up; past simple)
acceptedAnswers: ended up
exercises.feedback: Ended up + -ing reports the final outcome of the cancelled plan.

exercises.prompt: The designer ___ a website for the community garden last month. (set up; past simple)
acceptedAnswers: set up
exercises.feedback: Set up means establish the site. The past of set is also set.

exercises.prompt: Adil ___ in a fishing village before moving to the capital. (grow up; past simple)
acceptedAnswers: grew up
exercises.feedback: Grew up means spent his childhood there and became older.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The neighbours set on a shared tool library last year.
acceptedAnswers: The neighbours set up a shared tool library last year.
exercises.feedback: Set up a service means establish or create it.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The cyclist could not keep up the lead group on the hill.
acceptedAnswers: The cyclist could not keep up with the lead group on the hill.
exercises.feedback: Keep up with a group means maintain the same speed; the preposition with is required.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: After many failed lessons, he gave up to learn the instrument.
acceptedAnswers: After many failed lessons, he gave up learning the instrument.
exercises.feedback: Give up + -ing expresses stopping an activity or attempt.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We used up it before the next supply delivery arrived.
acceptedAnswers: We used it up before the next supply delivery arrived.
exercises.feedback: The pronoun it must appear between used and up.

speakingExercises.prompt: Paraphrase the supplied fact in the past simple: A visitor approached the reception desk. Begin "The visitor" and use walked up to.
acceptedAnswers: The visitor walked up to the reception desk.
speakingExercises.feedback: Walked up to expresses approaching a place or person.

speakingExercises.prompt: Mara was behind the other runners but eventually reached them. Say one sentence beginning "Mara" and using caught up with.
acceptedAnswers: Mara caught up with the other runners.
speakingExercises.feedback: Caught up with shows that Mara reached people who had been ahead.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two past-simple sentences using these facts. First: Elena / set up / a cycling club. Second: She / take up / cycling / last year.
acceptedAnswers: Elena set up a cycling club. She took up cycling last year.
speakingExercises.feedback: Set up establishes a club; took up means started an activity.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your hotel reservation failed, so your group stayed in a hostel. Say one sentence beginning "We" and using ended up staying at a hostel.
acceptedAnswers: We ended up staying at a hostel.
speakingExercises.feedback: Ended up staying describes the actual outcome, rather than the original plan.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are walking behind the guide and cannot maintain the guide’s speed. Tell the guide one complete sentence, beginning "I", using keep up with you.
acceptedAnswers: I can't keep up with you.
I cannot keep up with you.
speakingExercises.feedback: Keep up with describes maintaining another person’s speed.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the pronoun position and say the complete sentence, changing nothing else: "Please use up them before Friday."
acceptedAnswers: Please use them up before Friday.
speakingExercises.feedback: A pronoun object comes before up in use something up.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend says the community hall is untidy. Reply with one complete sentence beginning "We need" and ending "it up". Use the verb tidy.
acceptedAnswers: We need to tidy it up.
speakingExercises.feedback: Tidy it up means make the hall neat; the pronoun separates the verb and particle.

speakingExercises.prompt: Sam was expected at the workshop, but he did not arrive. Say one negative past-simple sentence beginning "Sam" and using show up.
acceptedAnswers: Sam didn't show up.
Sam did not show up.
speakingExercises.feedback: Show up means arrive or appear when expected.

listeningExercises.audioText: We started decorating late, and by sunset we had used up every tin of white paint.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the problem by sunset?
choices: The paint was the wrong colour.
listeningExercises.feedback: Used up every tin means the available paint was completely consumed.

listeningExercises.audioText: When Lia was young, her grandparents brought her up in a village beside the coast.
listeningExercises.prompt: Who raised Lia when she was a child?
listeningExercises.feedback: Brought her up identifies the people who raised and cared for her.

listeningExercises.audioText: Towards the end of the hike, I could barely keep up with the others.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word expression immediately after "barely".
acceptedAnswers: keep up with
listeningExercises.feedback: Keep up with describes maintaining the pace of those ahead.

listeningExercises.audioText: The organisers expected sixty visitors at the exhibition, but only thirty showed up.
choices: Only half the expected visitors arrived.
listeningExercises.feedback: Showed up means arrived; thirty is half the expected sixty.

listeningExercises.audioText: My neighbour introduced me to rock climbing, and I took it up during the summer break.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the speaker do during the summer?
listeningExercises.feedback: Took it up means began practising rock climbing as an activity.

listeningExercises.audioText: The training centre closed unexpectedly, so we ended up studying through online lessons instead.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the learners continue studying?
listeningExercises.feedback: Ended up describes the alternative arrangement that resulted from the closure.

listeningExercises.audioText: A few local families set up a reading room inside the old library.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase immediately after "families".
acceptedAnswers: set up
listeningExercises.feedback: Set up means established the reading room.

listeningExercises.audioText: The large old armchair takes up nearly half of the living room.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase immediately after "armchair".
acceptedAnswers: takes up
listeningExercises.feedback: Takes up means occupies an amount of space.
